transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

My mind keeps swinging between being full of plans and then feeling so foggy that I can’t focus long enough to finish anything. My primary care doctor suggested I come see you because these ups and downs are making it really hard to get anything done.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, and were more talkative or impulsive than usual?

Yes, I definitely have those highly energetic phases where I stay up super late working on projects and feel incredibly upbeat. During those times, my thoughts race like a bunch of browser tabs constantly popping open, and I talk in a nonstop stream so fast that my husband can't even get a word in. I'll take on way too many tasks at once, though I also notice I tend to snap at him easily over tiny things.
How long do these highly energetic, talkative periods usually last—do they go on for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least four days or longer?

Yes, those 'up' periods definitely last for weeks at a time, and during those weeks I feel incredibly revved up and active almost constantly throughout the day. It stays like that for a while before it eventually drops off into the low, foggy phases.
Have you ever had a full episode of depression—feeling down most of the day, nearly every day, with low energy, trouble concentrating, or loss of interest in things—for at least two weeks?

Yes, for about the last three months, I've been stuck in a low, foggy stretch most days where my energy feels completely drained, like my batteries are half-dead. During these times, I can't concentrate enough to read or write, and I've totally lost interest in things I normally love, like sketching and my book club.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F31", "F32", "F33"], but based on this conversation, F32 (episodic depressive disorder) and F33 (recurrent depressive disorder) are less likely because the patient reports distinct, persistent periods of abnormally elevated energy, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, increased talkativeness, and irritability lasting for weeks—meeting criteria for a manic episode. The presence of both full manic episodes (lasting weeks) and major depressive episodes supports a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder (F31). The pattern of cycling between mania and depression, rather than depression alone, rules out F32 and F33.
